newsitem.title: SWEDEN: European Federalists must come out of hiding - Rifkind.
newsitem.headline: European Federalists must come out of hiding - Rifkind.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Monday that Europeans seeking to build a federalist United States of Europe should come out of hiding and admit their preferences.
Rifkind, launching a series of European policy speeches, told reporters that German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac stated often they were not seeking a federal Europe.
"But what is the difference between what they are seeking and a federal Europe?" he asked reporters.

"Federalists must admit what they are," he added, saying London was bitterly opposed to extending the use in Brussels of majority voting, saying no proof had been given that such a voting system was worthwhile.

Rifkind was speaking in Sweden, whose centre-left minority government has developed sceptical views similar to London's to plans to deepen integration in the European Union (EU). Sweden joined the EU two years ago.
"In Stockholm...I am with people whose experience and outlook have something in common with our own in Britain," Rifkind said in a speech at Sweden's Foreign Policy Institute.
"Your prime minister recently pointed out that the Swedish people voted for a Europe that was inter-governmental not federal.
"He rightly warned that if further integration produced what would be, in effect, a federal Europe, that would not be the same EU that Sweden agreed to join. I profoundly agree with him," he said.
In a speech setting out what Rifkind called Britain's balanced approach to Europe, he said the EU should not be in a state of constant change.
"We need to show people that we are not in a state of perpetual revolution...I do not believe this pace of change can be sustained," he said.
Rifkind also attacked moves to hurry through European Monetary Union (EMU), saying a single European currency could only be introduced as a result "of fudging, of creative accounting."
"The main motors for the Euro are Germany and France, with the Benelux countries. If it does happen then it will have been due to creative accounting and fudging.
"The single currency...is unique. It has to be built on sound economic foundations. If it's not built on sound economic grounds then it will end in tears," he told a foreign press meeting.
Finance Minister Kenneth Clarke on Monday predicted the January 1, 1999 date for the launch of the Euro could soon be put back, saying EU states should temper their enthusiasm with common sense.
Rifkind said Britain was in favour of enlarging the EU to include formerly communist central and eastern European countries.
He said he hoped the Baltic countries of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia would be among the first to be ready to begin entry negotiations later this year.
